newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's SPD wants tax talks with CDU alone.
newsitem.headline: Germany's SPD wants tax talks with CDU alone.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said they were prepared to talk with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) about plans to reform tax laws and pension systems, a newspaper reported on Saturday.

The offer came a day after Kohl appealed to the party to help break a log jam in the planned reform. It also coincided with calls from the ruling coalition not to block its plans in the upper house of parliament, where the SPD holds a majority.
SPD parliamentary leader Peter Struck told Bild am Sonntag his party would be glad to meet the CDU for talks on condition its two coalition partners were not invited.
The exclusion of the CDU's Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and liberal Free Democrats (FDP), Struck said, was essential for constructive talks.

"It would be better... to meet behind closed doors to ensure that the tax reform goes ahead on time on January 1, 1998," Struck said in an interview released ahead of publication on Sunday. Such talks would speed up legislation, he said.

Kohl wants to slash income tax and corporate tax rates while scrapping 70 tax breaks in measures that would leave taxpayers 30 billion marks better off. But many CDU leaders oppose raising value-added tax to finance the cuts.

His Labour Minister Norbert Bluem unveiled plans last month to cut old-age pensions, raise contributions and launch a tax-financed "family fund" to keep the compulsory pensions scheme going in the 21st century -- but these were met with bitter criticism from junior coalition partner FDP.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl, who is also a member of the CDU, dismissed the SPD's proposal on talks arguing that until now the SPD had not been constructive, another newspaper Welt am Sonntag reported.

"There are too many voices. Negotiating with people who have no clear concept of their own would be very difficult," Bohl said in an interview excerpts of which were released ahead of Sunday's publication.
Bohl joined CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble and Finance Minister Theo Waigel in urging the SPD not to block the coalition's reform in the Bundesrat upper house.

Schaeuble told Welt am Sonntag that with joblessness at over 4.6 million -- a post-war record reached on Friday -- it brought home how urgently the reform was needed. He called on the SPD to avoid "saying 'no' in a petty way just to gain some small political advantage".
In remarks reported by the same paper, Waigel urged the SPD to consider the well-being of the whole nation and not merely the view of the party leadership.

Kohl said on Friday that if the SPD joined talks as well, he was confident a proposed tax and pension reform programme would get off the ground and help to stimulate economic growth and create new jobs.
